page.title: Lesson Overview
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 2 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Advanced Figurative Language and Mood

Lesson Focus

Primary standard: MLA.CW.POE.03—analyze and create patterns of advanced figurative language that deepen or shift mood.
Supporting standards: MLA.CW.POE.02 and MLA.CW.WR.05.

What You Will Learn

  • Trace an extended metaphor or image pattern across a poem.
  • Analyze how juxtaposition, ambiguity, sound, and a volta complicate mood.
  • Distinguish a mood shift from a random change in description.
  • Build a claim–evidence–reasoning analysis explaining interaction among devices.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 2 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task

Record every core term and its complete meaning in your writer’s notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context.

TermMeaningExample
extended metaphorA comparison developed across multiple lines or sections.A poem treats grief as winter through images of frost, bare branches, and thaw.
conceitAn elaborate, often surprising comparison that organizes a poem.A poem compares a crowded schedule to a constellation the speaker must navigate.
semantic fieldA group of words connected by a shared area of meaning.“Tide,” “shore,” “current,” and “anchor” create a semantic field of the sea.
juxtapositionPlacing contrasting images or ideas together to reveal a relationship.A warm kitchen is placed beside an empty, cold chair.
ambiguityLanguage supporting more than one reasonable interpretation.“I left the light on” may suggest welcome, fear, or unfinished hope.
synesthesiaImagery that blends two or more senses.“The trumpet’s bright note tasted like silver.”
motifA recurring image, phrase, sound, or idea.A cracked cup returns whenever the speaker remembers home.
voltaA meaningful turn in thought, mood, argument, or perspective.After describing loss, “But morning came” turns the poem toward possibility.
mood progressionThe way atmosphere develops across a text.Playful opening images gradually darken into an uneasy final scene.
tonal complexityThe coexistence or tension of more than one attitude.The speaker sounds affectionate about home while also criticizing its limits.
pattern breakA deliberate disruption that draws attention or signals change.A repeated refrain suddenly disappears in the final stanza.
cumulative effectThe combined impact produced by multiple related choices.Short lines, repeated hard sounds, and dark imagery together create pressure.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each meaning to the correct lesson term. Choose Check, review the correct matches, and retry. This is ungraded practice; no screenshot or extra submission is required.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Choose A or B before opening the feedback.

Which example is an extended metaphor?

A. “The moon was a coin.”

B. Across the poem, grief becomes winter through frost, bare branches, frozen ground, and an eventual thaw.

Check your choice and reasoning

B is correct. Its comparison develops through several connected images. A is a metaphor, but it appears only once and is not extended.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 2 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: Trace Patterns, Turns, and Mood

Six-Step Protocol

  1. Establish the baseline: name the opening literal situation and mood.
  2. Group the language: mark semantic fields such as weather, machinery, music, or illness.
  3. Trace the pattern: follow repeated comparison, image, object, or sound.
  4. Locate the turn: identify the word, line break, contrast, or discovery that redirects thought.
  5. Compare before and after: explain what changes and what remains.
  6. State the cumulative effect: connect the pattern and volta to a nuanced mood claim.

Visual Pattern Tracker

Before the voltaTurn signalAfter the voltaCumulative effect
closed-door images“yet”window/light imagesguarded hope

Pause and Choose: Locate the Volta

A poem repeats closed-door images, then begins a line with “yet” and introduces light through a window. Which explanation identifies the turn’s function?

A. “The volta occurs because ‘yet’ is an interesting transition word.”
Not the best choice. Naming the signal is only the first step. The answer must explain how the new image redirects the established pattern and mood.
B. “The word ‘yet’ marks a volta because the window light interrupts the closed-door pattern and makes an alternative to isolation visible.”
✓ Correct—the signal and structural change are connected. The response traces the earlier pattern, identifies the turning cue, and explains what the new image adds.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Learning Routes

  • Visual: use two colors for pre- and post-volta patterns.
  • Auditory: read aloud and listen for changed pace, repetition, or sound.
  • Hands-on: cut lines into strips; test where the turn is strongest.

Pause and Choose: State the Cumulative Mood

The closed-door imagery remains in memory after the window light appears. Which claim accounts for both continuity and change?

A. “The mood changes from sad to happy when the light appears.”
Not the best choice. The labels are vague, and a single new image does not erase the earlier guarded pattern.
B. “The mood progresses from guarded isolation to cautious hope because the light offers possibility while the remembered doors keep that hope uncertain.”
✓ Correct—the claim is cumulative and nuanced. It compares before and after, explains what remains, and names a precise mixed effect rather than replacing one mood with its opposite.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Analytical Frame

The recurring ___ initially suggests ___. At the volta, ___ changes the pattern by ___. Because the earlier association remains while the new image introduces ___, the mood progresses from ___ to ___, creating a cumulative effect of ___.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 2 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Advanced Patterns

Example 1 — Extended Metaphor

Lines: “I carried the apology like a sealed jar…At noon the lid began to sing…By evening, rain lived in my hands.”
Trace: The concealed apology is treated as a container under pressure. “Sing” blends sound with tension; the final rain suggests release.
Progression: restrained anxiety → unavoidable pressure → sorrowful relief.
Why it works: Each new image transforms the same conceit rather than adding unrelated decoration.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which explanation best traces the extended metaphor across the whole image?

A. The sealed jar is a creative comparison that makes the apology interesting.
Weaker response. This notices a comparison but does not trace how the conceit develops or changes the emotional progression.
B. The sealed jar turns the apology into contained pressure; the singing lid signals that the pressure can no longer remain hidden, and the rain in the speaker’s hands transforms restraint into sorrowful release.
Stronger response. This answer follows the same conceit through three linked images and explains how each stage changes the feeling.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Juxtaposition and Ambiguity

Lines: “Children chalk suns on the shelter wall / while sirens comb the avenue.”
Contrast: playful creation is placed beside danger.
Two readings: The suns may show resilient hope or innocence that cannot understand the threat.
Judgment: Both readings fit; the unresolved tension creates fragile, uneasy hope rather than uncomplicated optimism.

Example 3 — Pattern Break and Volta

Pattern: Four lines begin “We counted”—steps, coins, breaths, departures.
Break: The final line begins, “Then you stopped counting me.”
Reasoning: Repetition first creates control and shared ritual. The broken syntax turns counting into exclusion.
Cumulative effect: Order collapses into personal abandonment; the mood shifts from tense solidarity to isolation.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: Extend this metaphor by one line: “I carried the secret like a locked room.” Add a new image that develops—not abandons—the comparison, then explain the shift.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: One possible line is “By midnight, the key burned through my pocket.” The key continues the locked-room conceit and changes concealment into pressure to act.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 4 | Lesson 2 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Advanced Figurative Language and Mood

Purpose

Layer extended metaphor, personification, and imagery so mood shifts without becoming confusing.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Make deliberate choices that demonstrate the lesson skill.

Source for Your Work

Morning stitched gold along the rooftops, / but beneath the bridge the river / kept its iron voice.

1. Plan Before You Draft

Poetic DecisionYour Plan
Speaker, situation, and intended effectState each precisely.
Image or language patternList two connected possibilities.
Turn or developmentDescribe what changes and why.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger poetic craft? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Use unrelated comparisons in every line so the poem sounds highly figurative.
B. Develop a connected pattern of images, then alter one key image to signal a controlled change in mood.

3. Apply the Lesson

Create a 16–20 line poem or 300–350 word prose poem with a deliberate mood shift. Build an extended metaphor across at least three connected images and use one contrasting image at the turn.

4. Revise with Purpose

Revise the exact line where the mood changes. Explain how diction, sound, or image makes the turn perceptible.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your original writing applies the lesson skill and uses the supplied source or model.
  • Your explanation identifies a specific craft choice and its effect.
  • Your revision improves meaning or craft, not only spelling.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Advanced Figurative Language and Mood

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original writing, and explain your craft decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: After the Sirens

The neighborhood exhales through open windows. Porch lights bloom one by one, small moons returning after the storm. Somewhere, a broom whispers over broken glass, and morning balances on the rooftops—fragile, bright, unwilling to fall.

An extended metaphor develops a comparison across several related details. A motif is a recurring image or idea that helps unify meaning and mood.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. How do the images of breathing, blooming, and balancing work together to create an extended figurative pattern?
  2. Describe the mood shift in the passage. Which image marks the turn, and why is it effective?

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant word, line, or image, and explain how it proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which craft plan shows greater control of advanced figurative language?

A. Add many unrelated comparisons so every line sounds poetic.
B. Develop one connected image pattern and vary it at the turn so the figurative language supports a controlled mood shift.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Write an 18–24 line poem that develops an extended metaphor and a deliberate mood shift.

  1. Opening: Establish a concrete setting and the first part of the central comparison.
  2. Pattern: Extend the comparison through at least three related images without overexplaining it.
  3. Turn: Change the mood through a new perception, contrast, or reversal.
  4. Closing: Transform or echo an earlier image to leave a layered final impression.

Add a 100–150 word craft note explaining the metaphor, the mood before and after the turn, and the image that controls the shift.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the reader should experience, how each movement will build that effect, and which words and images will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Remove one image that competes with the central pattern, then strengthen a related image so the poem becomes more unified.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise the organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the writing becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The writing follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
